endorsements.quote: Patients should be informed when GenAI influences their care and have the opportunity to provide informed consent.

In the clinical encounters, students should form a preliminary plan, disclose any intended use of GenAI to the patient, and obtain informed consent before consulting GenAI (if needed) and then present their final clinical plan to faculty.
GenAI use must be documented in patient records.
Both faculty and students need education on algorithmic bias, data limitations, and the responsible use of AI.
Students and faculty should receive training on AI ethics and limitations before applying this knowledge in the clinic.
With respect to protected health information, dental schools must ensure students and faculty are using HIPAA‐compliant GenAI systems with institutional safeguards to protect privacy.
To enhance domain‐specific accuracy, future RLHF efforts should actively involve dental professionals in scoring and fine‐tuning model responses.

unlisted_practices: Require faculty review of the student's final clinical plan after any GenAI consultation.
Require AI use disclosure documentation in academic clinics when AI is used with patients.
Conduct regular audits of GenAI use documentation to provide feedback that informs future training and supervision.
Incorporate AI-specific ethics and safety training into didactic and clinical courses.
Ensure faculty calibration on AI to promote consistent messaging and modeling of ethical AI use.
Develop assessments that test students' critical thinking in the context of AI, such as explaining why an AI recommendation was accepted or rejected.
Foster an educational environment that promotes questioning, curiosity, and reflection.
Teach prompt engineering in curricula to optimize GenAI output.
Have students form a preliminary clinical plan before consulting GenAI.

screen.reason: This is an ethical commentary/viewpoint arguing for governance, faculty supervision, and patient informed consent regarding the chairside use of GenAI in dental clinics.
